title: Fleet telemetry
brief: A freight company has 150,000 trucks that each send a batch of sensor readings every 30 seconds. Dispatchers watch live maps and analysts run reports. You must take in every batch, keep a month of detail cheaply, and survive the moments when thousands of trucks come back online at once.

clarify.q: Can a batch from a truck be lost?
clarify.a: A minute of readings may be lost in a disaster, but not routinely. Batches are used for safety and billing reports.

clarify.q: How old can the live map data be?
clarify.a: A few seconds is fine. Reports can take several seconds to run.

clarify.q: How long do we keep the readings?
clarify.a: 30 days of full detail on fast storage, then the older data moves somewhere cheaper.

clarify.q: What do trucks do when they lose signal?
clarify.a: They keep the readings and upload the backlog when the signal returns, so reconnects arrive in bursts.

notes: Each telemetry batch holds about 100 readings, about 1 KB. 150,000 trucks every 30 s is about 5,000 batches a second.
About 500,000 readings a second at 1.5 bytes each compressed is around 65 GB a day (approx.).

numbers.label: Readings per second at peak
numbers.how: 5,580 batches/s x 100 readings (about 500,000 on an average second)

numbers.label: Hot storage for 30 days
numbers.how: 500,000 readings/s x 1.5 B x 86,400 s = 65 GB a day, x 30

hints: Trucks do not wait for an answer. What can accept a batch immediately and let the rest of the system work at its own pace?
A durable stream between the front door and the time-series database absorbs bursts. Add alerts on growth so storage never fills silently.
Balancer into an event stream (3 brokers), two stream workers into a 3-node time-series database, a small query API for dispatchers, metrics with an alert on series count and on disk growth.

editorial.summary: The load is steady, write-heavy and machine-made. Nobody is waiting for a reply, so the design is a pipe: accept fast, buffer in a stream, process, store in a database built for timestamps. The interesting failures are all about the pipe, not the users.

designs.name: Stream in front of a time-series store
designs.why: The stream accepts a burst of four times normal traffic and lets the workers catch up. The time-series database is built for this write rate and compresses readings. Alerts on series count and disk growth catch the two slow disasters before they cost money or stop writes.

tradeoffs: A stream costs a fixed amount each month. A per-message queue looks cheaper to start and costs more at this volume.
Short stream retention (one day) saves money but means a stuck worker must be fixed within a day or data is lost.
Moving data older than 30 days to the lake cuts storage cost by roughly ten times, but old reports run slower.
More partitions let more workers read in parallel; order is kept only inside one truck, which is all this problem needs.
Alerts cost a little and are the only reason a disk-full or label explosion is a small incident instead of a large one.
editorial.realWorld: Large fleets send on the order of one to ten readings a second per vehicle, and operators keep days to weeks on fast storage and years in cheap object storage (approx.).
